texts.text:
<definition id="fs-id1168329139829">
<term>base quantity</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1168326798190">physical quantity chosen by convention and practical considerations such that all other physical quantities can be expressed as algebraic combinations of them</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1168329127240">
<term>base unit</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1168329101575">standard for expressing the measurement of a base quantity within a particular system of units; defined by a particular procedure used to measure the corresponding base quantity</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1168326842432">
<term>derived units</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1168326841207">units that can be calculated using algebraic combinations of the fundamental units</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1168329175859">
<term>physical quantity</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1168329168545">characteristic or property of an object that can be measured or calculated from other measurements</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1168326860103">
<term>SI units</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1168329151186">the international system of units that scientists in most countries have agreed to use; includes units such as meters, liters, and grams</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1168329486946">
<term>units</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1168329063081">standards used for expressing and comparing measurements</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1168327920641">
<term>conversion factor</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1168328329236">a ratio that expresses how many of one unit are equal to another unit</meaning>
</definition>

<list id="fs-id1168328228670" list-type="bulleted" bullet-style="bullet">
<item>Every term in an expression must have the same dimensions; it does not make sense to add or subtract quantities of differing dimension (think of the old saying: “You can’t add apples and oranges”). In particular, the expressions on each side of the equality in an equation must have the same dimensions.</item>
<item>The arguments of any of the standard mathematical functions such as trigonometric functions (such as sine and cosine), logarithms, or exponential functions that appear in the equation must be dimensionless. These functions require pure numbers as inputs and give pure numbers as outputs.</item>
</list>

<definition id="fs-id1168327872808">
<term>dimension</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1168327908525">expression of the dependence of a physical quantity on the base quantities as a product of powers of symbols representing the base quantities; in general, the dimension of a quantity has the form <m:math><m:mrow><m:msup><m:mtext>L</m:mtext><m:mtext>a</m:mtext></m:msup><m:msup><m:mtext>M</m:mtext><m:mtext>b</m:mtext></m:msup><m:msup><m:mtext>T</m:mtext><m:mtext>c</m:mtext></m:msup><m:msup><m:mtext>I</m:mtext><m:mtext>d</m:mtext></m:msup><m:msup><m:mtext>Θ</m:mtext><m:mtext>e</m:mtext></m:msup><m:msup><m:mtext>N</m:mtext><m:mtext>f</m:mtext></m:msup><m:msup><m:mtext>J</m:mtext><m:mtext>g</m:mtext></m:msup></m:mrow></m:math> for some powers a, b, c, d, e, f, and g.</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1168328321073">
<term>dimensionless</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1168327949717">quantity with a dimension of <m:math><m:mrow><m:msup><m:mtext>L</m:mtext><m:mn>0</m:mn></m:msup><m:msup><m:mtext>M</m:mtext><m:mn>0</m:mn></m:msup><m:msup><m:mtext>T</m:mtext><m:mn>0</m:mn></m:msup><m:msup><m:mtext>I</m:mtext><m:mn>0</m:mn></m:msup><m:msup><m:mtext>Θ</m:mtext><m:mn>0</m:mn></m:msup><m:msup><m:mtext>N</m:mtext><m:mn>0</m:mn></m:msup><m:msup><m:mtext>J</m:mtext><m:mn>0</m:mn></m:msup><m:mo>=</m:mo><m:mn>1</m:mn><m:mo>;</m:mo></m:mrow></m:math> also called quantity of dimension 1 or a pure number</meaning>
</definition>

<para id="fs-id1168327924785">If either of these rules is violated, an equation is not dimensionally consistent and cannot possibly be a correct statement of physical law. This simple fact can be used to check for typos or algebra mistakes, to help remember the various laws of physics, and even to suggest the form that new laws of physics might take. This last use of dimensions is beyond the scope of this text, but is something you may learn later in your academic career.</para>

<definition id="fs-id1168328355532">
<term>accuracy</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1168328238378">the degree to which a measured value agrees with an accepted reference value for that measurement</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1168328328497">
<term>discrepancy</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1168327873821">the difference between the measured value and a given standard or expected value</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1168327927708">
<term>percent uncertainty</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1168328290905">the ratio of the uncertainty of a measurement to the measured value, expressed as a percentage</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1168328286055">
<term>precision</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1168328357317">the degree to which repeated measurements agree with each other</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1168327925704">
<term>significant figures</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1168328367297">used to express the precision of a measuring tool used to measure a value</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1168328241816">
<term>uncertainty</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1168328329079">a quantitative measure of how much measured values deviate from one another</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1167132688517">
<term>antiparallel vectors</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1167132688522">two vectors with directions that differ by <m:math><m:mrow><m:mn>180</m:mn><m:mtext>°</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:math></meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1167132504151">
<term>orthogonal vectors</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1167132504156">two vectors with directions that differ by exactly <m:math><m:mrow><m:mn>90</m:mn><m:mtext>°</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:math>, synonymous with perpendicular vectors</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1167132520196">
<term>parallel vectors</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1167132520201">two vectors with exactly the same direction angles</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1167132586350">
<term>scalar quantity</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1167132586355">quantity that can be specified completely by a single number with an appropriate physical unit</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1167132550493">
<term>vector</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1167132550498">mathematical object with magnitude and direction</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1167132579726">
<term>vector quantity</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1167132579731">physical quantity described by a mathematical vector—that is, by specifying both its magnitude and its direction; synonymous with a vector in physics</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1167132612567">
<term>direction angle</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1167132612572">in a plane, an angle between the positive direction of the <emphasis effect="italics">x</emphasis>-axis and the vector, measured counterclockwise from the axis to the vector</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1167132546151">
<term>vector components</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1167132266674">orthogonal components of a vector; a vector is the vector sum of its vector components.</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1167133549546">
<term>equal vectors</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1167133768492">two vectors are equal if and only if all their corresponding components are equal; alternately, two parallel vectors of equal magnitudes</meaning>
</definition>

<definition id="fs-id1167132506101">
<term>null vector</term>
<meaning id="fs-id1167133844322">a vector with all its components equal to zero</meaning>
</definition>
